title: Family and the people around you
title_target: かぞくは なんにんですか — Kazoku wa nannin desu ka
goal: Name family members with two different sets of words, count people and give ages, and describe others — their jobs, personalities and where they live.
bekal: telling your own family words from other people's
describing people with adjectives and jobs
asking about family without sounding nosy

dialogs.title: 会話 1 — How many in your family?
dialogs.intro: Tanaka asks about Ani's family. Look closely: the word for “mother” changes depending on whose mother it is.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [アニさんの|Ani-san no] [ごかぞくは|gokazoku wa] [なんにんですか|nannin desu ka]。
lines.id: Ani, how many people are in your family?
lines.literal: Ani-Ms. — 's — honorable-family — as-for — how-many-people — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [ごにん|Gonin] [かぞくです|kazoku desu]。[ちちと|Chichi to] [ははと|haha to] [あにと|ani to] [いもうとと|imōto to] [わたしです|watashi desu]。
lines.id: Five. My father, my mother, my older brother, my younger sister and me.
lines.literal: five-people — family — is. father — and — mother — and — older-brother — and — younger-sister — and — I — am.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [おにいさんは|Oniisan wa] [なんさいですか|nansai desu ka]。
lines.id: How old is your brother?
lines.literal: honorable-older-brother — as-for — how-many-years — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [あには|Ani wa] 28[さいです|sai desu]。[ジャカルタで|Jakaruta de] [はたらいています|hataraite imasu]。
lines.id: He's 28. He works in Jakarta.
lines.literal: older-brother — as-for — 28 — years — is. Jakarta — at — is-working.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [おしごとは|Oshigoto wa] [なんですか|nan desu ka]。
lines.id: What does he do?
lines.literal: honorable-work — as-for — what — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [いしゃです|Isha desu]。[とても|Totemo] [まじめな|majimena] [ひとです|hito desu]。
lines.id: He's a doctor. He's a very serious person.
lines.literal: doctor — is. very — serious — person — is.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [いもうとさんは|Imōtosan wa]？
lines.id: And your sister?
lines.literal: honorable-younger-sister — as-for?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [いもうとは|Imōto wa] [まだ|mada] [こうこうせいです|kōkōsei desu]。17[さいです|sai desu]。
lines.id: She's still in high school. She's 17.
lines.literal: younger-sister — as-for — still — high-school-student — is. 17 — years — is.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [ごりょうしんは|Goryōshin wa] [おげんきですか|ogenki desu ka]。
lines.id: Are your parents well?
lines.literal: honorable-parents — as-for — honorable-healthy — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[おかげさまで|okagesama de] [げんきです|genki desu]。[たなかさんの|Tanaka-san no] [ごかぞくは|gokazoku wa]？
lines.id: Yes, they're well, thank you. What about your family?
lines.literal: yes, honorable-thanks — by — healthy — is. Tanaka-Mr. — 's — honorable-family — as-for?

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [わたしは|Watashi wa] [ひとりっこです|hitorikko desu]。[りょうしんと|Ryōshin to] [さんにんです|sannin desu]。
lines.id: I'm an only child. It's just me and my parents.
lines.literal: I — as-for — only-child — am. parents — with — three-people — is.

notes: **Two sets of family words — the most distinctive feature of Japanese here.** For your own family, use the short, humble forms: **ちち** (my father), **はは** (my mother). For someone else's family, use the long, respectful forms: **おとうさん**, **おかあさん**. Using おかあさん for your own mother in front of outsiders sounds like you're praising your own family — which is exactly what's avoided.

**Inside the home, the rule flips.** You still call your mother おかあさん when talking **to her**. はは is only for talking about her **to outsiders**. This isn't about personal respect but about the in-group/out-group line (うち/そと) that governs much of Japanese.
**おかげさまで = “thanks to you”**, used as a polite reply when asked how you are. It doesn't mean the listener actually helped — it's a set phrase, used as reflexively as “fine, thanks”.
**ひとりっこ = only child.** Note the small つ (っ), which means a one-beat pause: hi-to-ri-k-ko.
**まだ = still**, and with a negative verb it means “not yet”: まだです (not yet). Two meanings, one word.

**はたらいています = works (there).** The ～ています form here expresses an **ongoing state** — a steady job, not a one-off activity. You'll hear it a lot for jobs and where people live: とうきょうに すんでいます (I live in Tokyo).

grammars.title: Two lists of family words
body: The left column is for **your own family** (when talking to outsiders). The right column is for **other people's families** — and also for addressing your own family members directly.
after: ⚠️ **Japanese always says which sibling is older.** There's no everyday word for just “brother” or “sister” without saying who's older — the opposite of English, where *brother* and *sister* don't tell you the order.
**If you forget, use the respectful form for other people.** Erring on the side of too much respect is far milder than being too familiar.

grammars.title: Counting people and ages
body: People are counted with **～[にん|nin] (人)**, ages with **～[さい|sai] ([歳|sai]/[才|sai])**. Both are regular except for a few forms you have to memorize.
after: ⚠️⚠️ **20 years old = [はたち|hatachi]**, which follows no pattern at all. The number matters in Japan: 20 was the legal age of adulthood under the old law and is still a social milestone.
**Ask about age with care.** [なんさいですか|nansai desu ka] is fine for children and peers, but best avoided entirely with older people. The polite form is **[おいくつですか|oikutsu desu ka]**.

dialogs.title: 会話 2 — Describing someone
dialogs.intro: Ani introduces a classmate through a photo. Notice how adjectives and nouns are chained to describe people.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [この|Kono] [しゃしんの|shashin no] [ひとは|hito wa] [だれですか|dare desu ka]。
lines.id: Who's the person in this photo?
lines.literal: this — photo — 's — person — as-for — who — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [クラスの|Kurasu no] [ともだちです|tomodachi desu]。[なまえは|Namae wa] [マヤさんです|Maya-san desu]。
lines.id: A friend from class. Her name is Maya.
lines.literal: class — 's — friend — is. name — as-for — Maya-Ms. — is.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [どんな|Donna] [ひとですか|hito desu ka]。
lines.id: What's she like?
lines.literal: what-kind-of — person — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [あかるくて|Akarukute]、[しんせつな|shinsetsuna] [ひとです|hito desu]。[かみが|Kami ga] [ながいです|nagai desu]。
lines.id: She's cheerful and kind. She has long hair.
lines.literal: cheerful-and, kind — person — is. hair — [subject] — long — is.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [マヤさんも|Maya-san mo] [インドネシアじんですか|Indoneshia-jin desu ka]。
lines.id: Is Maya Indonesian too?
lines.literal: Maya-Ms. — also — Indonesia-person — is — [question].

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、[スラバヤから|Surabaya kara] [きました|kimashita]。[いま|Ima] [おおさかに|Ōsaka ni] [すんでいます|sunde imasu]。
lines.id: Yes, she's from Surabaya. Now she lives in Osaka.
lines.literal: yes, Surabaya — from — came. now — Osaka — in — is-living.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [そのとなりの|Sono tonari no] [ひとは|hito wa]？
lines.id: And the person next to her?
lines.literal: that — next-to — 's — person — as-for?

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [せんせいです|Sensei desu]。[きびしいですが|Kibishii desu ga]、[いい|ii] [せんせいです|sensei desu]。
lines.id: Our teacher. Strict, but a good teacher.
lines.literal: teacher — is. strict — is — but, good — teacher — is.

lines.speaker: たなか:
lines.text: [せが|Se ga] [たかいですね|takai desu ne]。
lines.id: He's tall, isn't he?
lines.literal: height — [subject] — high — is — right.

lines.speaker: アニ:
lines.text: [はい|Hai]、190[センチ|senchi] [ぐらいです|gurai desu]。[バスケットボールが|Basukettobōru ga] [じょうずです|jōzu desu]。
lines.id: Yes, about 190 centimeters. He's great at basketball.
lines.literal: yes, 190 — centimeters — about — is. basketball — [subject] — skilled — is.

notes: **せがたかい = tall (person), not just たかい.** たかいひと could read as “an expensive person”. For height, せ (stature) is the subject: せがたかい / せがひくい.
**Body parts and traits use the ～が～です pattern.** かみがながい (has long hair), めがおおきい (has big eyes), あたまがいい (is smart — literally “head is good”). The person described takes は, the part takes が.
**すんでいます = live (reside).** Always in the ～ています form, never すみます, when saying where you live. The place is marked with **に**: とうきょうに すんでいます.
**あかるくて — い-adjectives link with ～くて.** あかるい + しんせつ = あかるくて、しんせつな. な-adjectives link with で: しんせつで、あかるい.
**きびしい = strict, demanding.** For teachers and bosses this isn't an insult — it's often praise mixed with respect.
**センチ = centimeter**, from *centimeter*. Height in Japan is always given in whole centimeters: 170センチ, not 1.7 meters.

grammars.title: Linking two adjectives
body: To give one thing or person two qualities, the first adjective changes into a linking form. The form depends on the type of adjective.

head: Type
How
Example
rows: [やすくて|Yasukute] [おいしい|oishii] — cheap and tasty
[しずかで|Shizuka de] [きれい|kirei] — quiet and clean
[がくせいで|Gakusei de] 20[さい|sai] — a student, and 20
[よくて|Yokute] [やすい|yasui] — good and cheap

after: ⚠️ **This link is only for qualities that point the same way.** If they contrast (expensive but tasty), use **[が|ga]** = but: [たかいです|takai desu]**[が|ga]**、[おいしいです|oishii desu]。 Using [くて|kute] for contrasting qualities sounds odd to Japanese ears.

grammars.title: Describing people
body: The most natural order: **quality → person → extra details**. Note that [な|na]-adjectives need [な|na] before [ひと|hito]; [い|i]-adjectives don't.

head: Quality
Meaning
Sentence
rows: [きびしい|Kibishii] [せんせいです|sensei desu]。
[まじめな|Majimena] [がくせいです|gakusei desu]。

head: Physical trait
Sentence
Meaning
rows: [かみが|Kami ga] [ながいです|nagai desu]。
[めが|Me ga] [おおきいです|ōkii desu]。
[あたまが|Atama ga] [いいです|ii desu]。

after: **Avoid physical comments.** In Japan, commenting on the weight, age or looks of someone you've just met is considered very rude — and the bar is high. When in doubt, stick to personality and job.

blocks.text: All of these work with the simple pattern you've known since Unit 1: **[who] は [job] です**.

blocks.title: ⚠️ せんせい isn't used for yourself
items: せんせい is a **title of respect** that others give you. Saying “わたしはせんせいです” about yourself sounds like you're demanding respect.
If you are a teacher, call yourself **きょうし** (教師) — the neutral word for the profession.
The same pattern runs through all of Japanese: respectful forms for others, neutral or humble forms for yourself. You've seen it with family in this unit, and with さん in Unit 1.

blocks.text: In Japan, questions about family are handled much more carefully than in many other cultures. Safe things to ask a new acquaintance:

head: Safe to ask
Sentence
rows: [ごかぞくは|Gokazoku wa] [なんにんですか|nannin desu ka]。
[きょうだいは|Kyōdai wa] [いますか|imasu ka]。
[どこに|Doko ni] [すんでいますか|sunde imasu ka]。
[おしごとは|Oshigoto wa] [なんですか|nan desu ka]。

head: Better avoided
Why
rows: Seen as private, especially with women.
A common question in some cultures, but it feels pushy in Japan.

blocks.title: If you're the one being asked
items: You don't have to answer in full. **[ちょっと|Chotto]…** is enough to close the question without offending — and Japanese people will get it right away.
Or, if you want to change the subject: answer briefly, then turn the question around with **[～さんは|～-san wa]？** — a pattern you've used since Unit 1.

vocab.ja: [すんでいます|sunde imasu] 住んでいます
vocab.baca: すんでいます · sunde imasu

vocab.ja: [はたらいています|hataraite imasu] 働いています
vocab.baca: はたらいています · hataraite imasu
